notes.short: A number set as a riddle that calls for wisdom
notes.about: The verse does not name the beast plainly. It gives a number, and says, “Here is a call for wisdom.” The one with insight is to calculate it, for it is the number of a man. The number is set like a riddle, to be worked out with wisdom and understanding.

figure.name: Riddle
figure.means: something of the beast hidden in a number, which verse 17 ties to its name; the verse calls for wisdom and insight to work it out

notes.evidence: Albert Barnes calls the number enigmatical, tied to the beast’s name, and says working it out takes the skill a riddle needs. William Tong (Matthew Henry’s Commentary) says it is given so as to exercise all the wisdom of men. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says spiritual wisdom is needed against the mystery of iniquity, and that the verse implies the number can be counted.
notes.limit: The note gives no answer to the riddle.

cites.quote: the number was so far enigmatical as to require much skill in determining its meaning. ... The plain meaning is, that the number 666 would be so connected with his name ... that it could be determined who was meant ... This is the exercise of the skill or wisdom to which the writer here refers: substantially that which is required in the solution of a riddle or a conundrum.

cites.quote: We have here the number of the beast, given in such a manner as shows the infinite wisdom of God, and will sufficiently exercise all the wisdom and accuracy of men: The number is the number of a man, computed after the usual manner among men, and it is 666.
Spiritual wisdom is needed to solve the mystery of iniquity, so as not to be beguiled by it. ... The "for" implies the possibility of our calculating or counting the beast's number.
